key_insight: The paper shows that simulator calibration and reinforcement learning for urban traffic can be tied together through a shared learned latent space. In simple terms, it learns a compact traffic representation that helps both match simulations to reality and control city traffic more effectively.
problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of optimizing urban transportation networks, where practitioners must both calibrate high-fidelity traffic simulators to real-world data and make real-time control decisions under complex, dynamic conditions.
method: Builds a combinatorial MLP-autoencoder that compresses urban traffic simulator inputs into a low-dimensional latent manifold.
Uses the shared latent representation to connect simulator calibration with reinforcement learning-based control policies.
Learns a common traffic dynamics space that supports both parameter fitting and operational decision-making in urban networks.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a way to unify model calibration and control instead of treating them as separate problems. It can improve sample efficiency, reduce manual tuning, and make learned policies more transferable to complex real-world systems.
visual_elements: A pipeline diagram showing simulator inputs flowing into a latent-space autoencoder and then into calibration and control branches.

A side-by-side comparison of calibrated simulation output versus observed traffic data.
paper_title: Learning to Move Cities: Deep Meta-Models and Reinforcement Policies for Calibration and Control in Urban Networks
paper_authors: Adewumi Augustine Adepitan, Christopher J. Haruna, Oluwasegun Adegoke, Ayooluwatomiwa Ajiboye, Oluwatobi Oluwasakin
